question:
Democracy is often imagined as a contest of numbers, in which the side commanding the larger count prevails. Yet the deeper purpose of democratic institutions is not merely to register the preference of the majority but to ensure that power, once conferred, remains answerable. A government that wins an election and thereafter governs without restraint has satisfied only the arithmetic of democracy, not its spirit. The genius of constitutional design lies in dispersing authority — between the legislature and the executive, between the union and its provinces, between the state and an independent judiciary — so that no single organ may claim to embody the popular will in its entirety. Decentralization, in this view, is not a concession grudgingly made to regional sentiment but a structural safeguard. When decisions are taken close to those they affect, the citizen ceases to be a distant spectator and becomes a participant whose voice carries weight. The price of such dispersal is a certain slowness; consensus is harder to assemble, and bold action is more easily obstructed. But this friction is not a defect to be engineered away. It is the cost a society pays for keeping power perpetually accountable, and it is a price worth paying.

Q: The central idea of the passage is that:
options: (a) The dispersal of authority, though it slows governance, keeps power accountable
(b) Decentralization is merely a concession made to satisfy regional sentiment
(c) An elected government should be free to govern without any restraint
(d) Democracy is essentially a method of counting majority preferences
explanation: The passage argues dispersal of power is a structural safeguard whose cost (slowness) is worth paying for accountability.
subject: CSAT

question:
India's electricity system is undergoing a transition whose pace has surprised even its planners. By the middle of 2025 the share of installed capacity drawn from non-fossil sources had crossed the halfway mark, a threshold the country had pledged to reach only by 2030 under its international climate commitments. Yet installed capacity is a deceptive measure. A solar park rated at a thousand megawatts produces nothing after sunset and little under heavy cloud; the figure records potential, not delivery. The genuine difficulty of the transition lies not in building generators but in matching a variable supply to a demand that peaks in the evening, precisely when the sun has gone. Storage — in batteries, in pumped reservoirs of water lifted uphill by surplus daytime power — is therefore the hinge on which the whole enterprise turns. Without it, a grid rich in renewable capacity must still keep fossil plants idling in reserve, ready to cover the gap, and the emissions saved on paper are partly lost in practice. The headline number, in short, marks a beginning, not an arrival.

Q: The author argues that installed capacity is a "deceptive measure" because it:
options: (a) Is calculated only at the middle of the year
(c) Records potential output rather than electricity actually delivered
(d) Excludes the contribution of fossil-fuel plants
explanation: 'The figure records potential, not delivery' — a solar park produces nothing after sunset.
subject: CSAT

question:
Each wave of automation has been accompanied by a familiar prophecy: that machines will at last exhaust the supply of human work. The prophecy has so far proved wrong, not because technology fails to displace particular tasks — it plainly does — but because the same advances that destroy certain kinds of work tend to enlarge the demand for others. A tool that makes one worker more productive lowers the cost of what she produces, and cheaper goods free income that is then spent on services scarcely imagined before. What is different about the present moment is the breadth of the tasks now exposed. Earlier machines automated the predictable and the routine; the newest systems reach into territory once thought to be the preserve of judgement — drafting, diagnosing, designing. This does not guarantee mass unemployment, for the historical mechanism of compensation may operate as it always has. But it does mean that the transition could be sharper and more concentrated than before, falling heavily on a few occupations within a short span, and the adequacy of any society's response will be measured less by the eventual equilibrium than by how it cushions those caught in the interval.

Q: The "familiar prophecy" mentioned by the author refers to the belief that:
options: (a) Machines will eventually eliminate the supply of human work
(b) Cheaper goods free income for new services
(c) New technologies are confined to routine tasks
(d) Automation always enlarges the demand for human work
explanation: The prophecy is 'that machines will at last exhaust the supply of human work'.
subject: CSAT

question:
A decade ago, the unbanked Indian transacted almost entirely in cash, and the small merchant kept accounts in a ledger that no institution could see. The arrival of a unified, interoperable payments system changed this with unusual speed: by the end of 2025 the network was processing more than twenty billion transactions in a single month, a volume without parallel anywhere in the world. The significance, however, lies less in the count than in what the count makes possible. Every digital transaction leaves a trace, and a trail of traces is, in effect, a credit history. A vegetable seller who once could borrow only from a moneylender at ruinous rates can now present a verifiable record of daily turnover to a formal lender. The same infrastructure that moves small sums cheaply thus quietly assembles the data on which inclusion in the wider financial system depends. Critics warn, rightly, that such a trail can also be a means of surveillance, and that the convenience is not costless. But to the seller who gains access to fair credit for the first time, the ledger that anyone may inspect is also a ledger that finally counts in her favour.

Q: The author maintains that the chief significance of the payments system lies in:
options: (a) Its being without parallel anywhere in the world
(b) The sheer number of monthly transactions it processes
(c) The data trail it generates, which can serve as a credit history
(d) Its replacement of the traditional moneylender
explanation: 'The significance… lies less in the count than in what the count makes possible' — a credit history.
subject: CSAT

question:
The most recent national assessment records that forest and tree cover together now extend over roughly a quarter of the country's land. Read alone, the figure invites complacency, for it has crept upward across successive surveys. But an aggregate conceals as much as it reveals. A hectare of dense, old-growth forest and a hectare of young plantation are counted alike, though they differ enormously in the carbon they hold, the species they shelter, and the water they regulate. Much of the recorded increase comes from plantations and orchards on the margins, even as the richest forests of the interior are nibbled at by roads, mines and the slow encroachment of cultivation. To measure conservation by total cover is therefore to mistake quantity for quality. A wiser accounting would weigh each hectare by what it sustains, and would treat the loss of an ancient forest as a debt that no quantity of saplings can immediately repay.

Q: The author's main contention is that:
options: (a) Total forest cover is a misleading measure because it ignores quality
(b) Plantations are ecologically equivalent to old-growth forests
(c) The national assessment exaggerates the extent of forest cover
(d) The country's total forest cover has been declining steadily
explanation: 'To measure conservation by total cover is… to mistake quantity for quality.'
subject: CSAT

question:
It is tempting to suppose that we first have thoughts, fully formed and silent within us, and only afterwards dress them in words for the benefit of others. On this picture language is a mere garment, and a clumsy one, forever failing to fit the thought beneath. Yet anyone who has struggled to articulate a half-grasped idea knows that the labour of finding words is often the labour of forming the thought itself. The sentence does not report a meaning that preceded it; it brings that meaning into focus, the way a developing photograph brings an image out of a blur. This is not to say that thought is nothing but inner speech, for we can mean more than we manage to say, and a gesture or a silence may carry what no sentence captures. But the common assumption — that the thought is the master and the word its servant — understates how far the available words shape what can be thought at all. A people whose language draws a distinction we lack may, quite literally, notice what we overlook.

Q: The "tempting" supposition the author describes is that:
options: (a) Words always fit the thoughts beneath them
(b) Language shapes the thoughts we are able to have
(c) Thoughts exist fully formed before being expressed in words
(d) Thought is nothing more than inner speech
explanation: The tempting view: 'we first have thoughts, fully formed… and only afterwards dress them in words.'
subject: CSAT

A people whose language draws a distinction we lack may, quite literally, notice what we overlook.

Q: The author qualifies his position by conceding that:
options: (b) Thought is entirely identical to inner speech
(c) We can sometimes mean more than we manage to say
explanation: 'We can mean more than we manage to say, and a gesture or a silence may carry what no sentence captures.'
subject: CSAT

question:
It is tempting to suppose that we first have thoughts, fully formed and silent within us, and only afterwards dress them in words for the benefit of others. On this picture language is a mere garment, and a clumsy one, forever failing to fit the thought beneath. Yet anyone who has struggled to articulate a half-grasped idea knows that the labour of finding words is often the labour of forming the thought itself. The sentence does not report a meaning that preceded it; it brings that meaning into focus, the way a developing photograph brings an image out of a blur. This is not to say that thought is nothing but inner speech, for we can mean more than we manage to say, and a gesture or a silence may carry what no sentence captures. But the common assumption — that the thought is the master and the word its servant — understates how far the available words shape what can be thought at all. A people whose language draws a distinction we lack may, quite literally, notice what we overlook.

Q: The example of "a people whose language draws a distinction we lack" supports the claim that:
options: (a) Thought is the master and the word its servant
(d) The words available to us shape what we are able to notice and think
explanation: Such a people 'may, quite literally, notice what we overlook' — vocabulary shapes perception/thought.
subject: CSAT

question:
There is an old reassurance that a rising tide lifts all boats, and for long stretches of history it has held: sustained economic growth has pulled hundreds of millions out of poverty more surely than any programme of redistribution. The reassurance becomes misleading, however, when it is used to dismiss the distribution of gains as irrelevant. Two economies may grow at the same rate while one delivers most of the increase to those already prosperous and the other spreads it broadly; the average conceals the difference. Moreover, where the gains concentrate, they tend to translate into political influence, and influence is used to shape the rules — over taxation, over the terms of competition, over access to opportunity — in ways that entrench the very concentration that produced it. Growth, in other words, is necessary but not self-justifying. The relevant question is not merely how fast an economy expands but who is positioned to capture what it produces, for an expansion whose fruits are captured narrowly can erode the conditions of its own continuation.

Q: The author's primary purpose is to argue that:
options: (a) Economic growth is irrelevant to reducing poverty
(b) The distribution of growth's gains matters, not just the rate of growth
(c) Redistribution is always superior to growth
(d) A rising tide always lifts all boats equally
explanation: Growth is 'necessary but not self-justifying'; who captures the gains is the relevant question.
subject: CSAT

question: In a certain code TEACHER is written as VGCEJGT. How is STUDENT written in that code?
explanation: Each letter is shifted +2. S->U, T->V, U->W, D->F, E->G, N->P, T->V gives UVWFGPV.

question: Pointing to a photograph, a man said, "I have no brother or sister, but that man's father is my father's son." Whose photograph was it?
explanation: 'My father's son' = the man himself (he has no brother). So that man's father is the speaker -> the photo is of his son.
subject: CSAT

question: A man walks 5 km north, turns right and walks 3 km, turns right and walks 5 km, then turns left and walks 4 km. How far and in which direction is he from the start?
explanation: Net: N5 then S5 cancel (y back to 0); E3 then E4 = 7 km east. Distance 7 km, due East.
subject: CSAT

question: Statements: All poets are dreamers. Some dreamers are realists. Conclusions: I. Some poets are realists. II. Some realists are dreamers. Which follow?
explanation: II is the valid converse of 'some dreamers are realists'. I is not certain — the realist-dreamers need not be poets.
subject: CSAT

question: Statements: No scientist is dishonest. All chemists are scientists. Conclusions: I. No chemist is dishonest. II. Some scientists are chemists. Which follow?
explanation: Chemists ⊆ scientists and no scientist is dishonest -> no chemist is dishonest (I). 'All chemists are scientists' converts to 'some scientists are chemists' (II). Both follow.
subject: CSAT

question: Six friends S, Q, R, P, T and U sit in a row facing north. R is third from the left. P sits immediately to the right of R. S is at the extreme left. Q sits between S and R. T is not at the extreme right end. Who sits at the extreme right end?
explanation: Order fixes as S(1) Q(2) R(3) P(4); T cannot be 6, so T=5 and U=6. U is at the extreme right.

question: If 8 June 2026 is a Monday, what day of the week will 8 June 2027 be?

explanation: Falling solar cost plus rising coal cost implies relative cost-competitiveness improved; the others overreach.

question: In a class, Ravi is 7th from the top and 26th from the bottom. How many students are in the class?

question: You are a junior officer. Your senior verbally instructs you to clear a file that you believe violates a financial rule. The most appropriate course of action is to:
options: (a) Approve it at once, since seniors must be obeyed
(b) Refuse outright and report the senior to the anti-corruption bureau
(c) Record your reservations in writing, seek clarification, and proceed only if the objection is satisfactorily resolved
(d) Quietly sit on the file indefinitely without informing anyone
explanation: Balances rule-compliance with respect for hierarchy: noting objections in writing protects both the institution and the officer.
subject: CSAT

question: As a team leader you find that a personal conflict between two members is affecting work. You would:
options: (a) Reprimand both in front of the entire team
(b) Ignore it, as personal matters are none of your concern
(c) Speak to each privately, understand the issue, and mediate to restore a professional working relationship
(d) Immediately transfer one of them to another team
explanation: Private, empathetic mediation addresses the cause while preserving dignity and team functioning.
subject: CSAT

question: You discover that your office made a small billing error that overcharged a citizen who has not noticed. You would:
options: (a) Quietly adjust the records so no one finds out
(b) Wait until the citizen complains, then act
(c) Do nothing, since the amount is small and unnoticed
(d) Inform the citizen, apologise, and arrange a refund of the excess
explanation: Integrity and accountability require proactively correcting the error and refunding the citizen.
subject: CSAT

question: Midway through a deadline-bound project you realise the original plan has a flaw that will cause problems later, though fixing it will delay delivery. The best approach is to:
options: (a) Press on with the flawed plan to meet the deadline and deal with problems later
(b) Inform stakeholders of the flaw and its implications, and jointly decide whether to revise the plan or the timeline
(c) Fix it secretly and hope the delay goes unnoticed
explanation: Transparent escalation lets stakeholders make an informed trade-off between scope, quality and time.
subject: CSAT

question: A close friend asks you, a government official, for confidential information that would benefit their business. You would:
options: (a) Share only part of the information to keep the friend content
(b) Pretend you do not have access to such information
(c) Share it, because the friendship matters
(d) Politely decline, explaining that the information is confidential and sharing it would be improper
explanation: Declining honestly while explaining the duty of confidentiality upholds integrity without deceit.
subject: CSAT

question: During a public emergency you receive two urgent but conflicting instructions from two different superiors. You should:
options: (a) Follow the instruction of whichever superior you like more
(b) Ignore both and act entirely on your own
(c) Quickly seek clarification from both; if they are unreachable, act on the option that best serves public safety and document the decision
(d) Do nothing until the conflict is resolved
explanation: Attempt to reconcile the orders; absent that, public safety is the overriding criterion, with the decision recorded for accountability.
subject: CSAT
